threads.title: Is Feedback On Your Bots Actually Useful

messages.author: JaaShooUhh
messages.content:
Is feedback on your bots ACTUALLY valuable?


Cause lets take a moment to expand on this.


If we factor in all the different things that can affect the feedback, it does feel like the ONLY actually useful feedback one can give, would be on the presentation of the bot itself.

Such as pointing out grammar, spelling, and markdown errors.


Aside from that, I'm not sure feedback from people is actually valuable unless users are FORCED to play your bots a certain way.


Lets think about it for a moment.


These things can all affect how a user experiences your bot:

1. AI MODEL + settings
What model they are using and what their temperatures (top-p, top-k, etc) are all set at can DRASTICALLY and COMPLETELY change a bot entirely. I've experienced this even as a free user, where some AI models will ignore or hyperfocus on specific aspects of your bots personality, to the point it overrides the desired outcome.

2. PERSONA
Our personas can HEAVILY affect how bots treat us. I've experienced this first hand by being completely honest about who I am as a person and making it my persona info. Upon doing so, some bots that I talked to prior, immediately began treating me differently simply because I put "diagnosed sociopath" in my persona.

3. LOREBOOKS + MEMORY
Keep in mind, each of us experience all these bots at different levels of memory, and if some of us cannot or do not trigger lorebook entries (and those entries actually are useful), then our experiences will also vary heavily. Once again, from a first hand experience, I have tested other people's bots before and after learning about their lorebooks, and I can say, that not knowing what to say and how to say it to make the bot use the entry as intended, can cause a lot of miscommunication and even fully derail a roleplay from reaching an intended goal.

messages.author: JaaShooUhh
messages.content:
4. USER'S OWN BEHAVIOR
Another thing to remember is HOW people roleplay. For example, if the user does not stick to the pre-written plot or personality, it can fully derail a bot. I know this from experience, as I will ONLY ever roleplay as myself, and any time a bot is like "you're X and you act like X", I'm just like "uhh, no... how about go fuck yourself". So once again, this can also heavily change a user's experience, and give them a false impression of your bot.

5. USER'S OWN PREFERENCES
Many times I will encounter a bot that isn't fully fleshed out to tell me upfront what its purpose is for, often leading to a NEGATIVE experience because people like to keep their bots as vague as possible with some details. A prime example is the amount of bots that are written as a "married partner". Now, unless the bot says "this character is NOT married to you", you'd assume they probably are. I've experienced this multiple times, where a bot's personality is hidden and their greeting is vague enough for you to think "oh okay, so I'm probably their significant other", then like 10 or 50 messages in, suddenly its like "by the way, I'm already taken by someone else", and for me, its a big slap in the face to who I am as a person (i.e. I HATE INFIDELITY).

messages.author: JaaShooUhh
messages.content:
6. USER'S EXPECTATIONS
One thing people forget, is as your bot gets MORE POPULAR, the expectations of people also increases. This is a common "bandwagoning" effect, where we are more likely to look at the thing with the BIGGER NUMBER, but then our expectations also increase. The same applies to tokens or seeing a bot that has a lorebook attached. The reality is, everything has a bigger perspective shift than you'd expect. If I see a 1000 token bot, I'm already thinking "ah, I bet this person put in a LOT of work". Same if I see a bot with a lorebook. On that same side, if I see less than 500 tokens, my expectations are MUCH LOWER. To further add to this, TAGS also change people's expectations. For example, if I see a bot with the VORE tag, my IMMEDIATE assumption is that at some point, the bot will FORCIBLY eat me against my will, and all roads lead to that outcome eventually.


So, is feedback from users actually useful?

Honestly, probably not. There are too many variables to account for, and too many things that can fully ruin the presentation of a bot.

While i get the whole aspect that theres a million variables to feedback itself, the feedback also has to account for these. Saying "I had a nice time" or "The character doesnt work because X" has little to no value.

Feedback in my opinion is best delivered with necesary context, "I met character X and did Y, it was pleasnt or bad or whatever, because he/she is this way or did that when this happened" As the creator you would get to see both that your bot handled a scenario that you could not have planned for in advance maybe and what the result was.

Negative feedback however is harder to gauge, recently i had a bot break because i made it hit the guard rails stupidly, that is on me, but i wish i knew earlier because in my eyes when i made and tested her, she worked from start to finish perfectly fine. So negative feedback can come also with its needed context so that persona, scenario and a lot of the variables can be stripped, leaving the creator with a clearer choice of "This character works perfectly even if you didnt like it" or "That really doesnt fit her or is not suppsoed to happen"

messages.author: Akira1992
messages.content:
All I can say is that feedback is useful when it provides information.

For example, let's say you get feedback like, "Hey, I thought the bot was really cute and had a hot avatar." Or, "Another crappy hard NTR bot, do something new!"
Useless feedback that's purely an opinion about the bot.

So, feedback would be useful if it sounded like this: "Hey, I really liked the story behind it, and the way it developed slowly was a good idea." "The bot was incredibly good at staying in character the whole time." "Hey, your bot drifts off course really quickly." Or, "Your bot just goes around in circles and doesn't respond to anything."

So, feedback isn't an opinion, but a description of performance. For example, I have my bots tested, receive feedback, and make changes accordingly. So, to answer the question of whether feedback is useful, it's only if it's genuine feedback and not just a comment.

messages.author: JaaShooUhh
messages.content:
Yeah, but aren't these things affected by the AI models and {{user}}'s subscription?

Like, imagine you have dozens of people telling you "your bot forgets who she is too soon and doesn't stay in character", but all of them have their AI model settings set to weird things that just break the bot.

Then you, as the creator, are given a FALSE IMPRESSION of your bot, because the information you are given, while true to some degree, is based on a {{user}}'s own doing.

It'd be like a car dealership being told that all their cars don't work, but the drivers never switch the car out of park because they assume it should always be in drive.

There is only so much you can ACTUALLY manage and account for, before something breaks.


A good example is that prior to my new account and bot style, I used to make hundreds of female bots.

One of them was strictly written as being deaf.

Now, under the default model, she worked just fine. Responded like she was actually deaf and never responded to dialogue.

However, the moment I switched her to a different model, she started responding to dialogue.

I didn't change the coding, I didn't do anything besides change the AI model.

So had OTHER people used her with the wrong model, then I would have been told by people "I thought you said she was deaf, she responds to me when I speak".

So then I would try to FIX the non-broken bot, to adjust to a different AI model or all the criticism, and possibly break her for both models or the current one she works best with.

Seems like a neverending cycle.

messages.author: Akira1992
messages.content: So the best solution would be to buy a new one (for the Car)... or delete the bot / set it to unlisted and upload a fresh, new version.

messages.author: Akira1992
messages.content: And ultimately, if I want to play with a bot of my own, I do it using a private version anyway; that way, I can modify the scenario as we go and handle memory manipulation more effectively, allowing for chats exceeding 1,000 messages without any issues.

messages.author: JaaShooUhh
messages.content:
Yes, but the original question was "does feedback actually matter"?

If the results are always inconsistent or based on false impressions, then feedback would actually be MORE HARMFUL because the feedback, even if positive, could be positive for all the wrong reasons, and if negative, could be negative for reasons that the creator cannot fix.

Hence why I said, aside from fixing clearly noticeable errors, such as spelling and grammar and markdown, all other feedback is not only subjective, but not actually beneficial or superficially beneficial.

messages.author: JaaShooUhh
messages.content:
Hence the Deaf example I gave.

My bot, under a specific model, works just fine.

Under a different model, does not.

So as a creator, I would then have to assume that all feedback of the "deafness" not working, are from {{user}} error, when in fact, it could be my own error.

But there is no way to know, because using the default model works just fine, but at some point, it could just fuck up for no reason.

messages.author: Akira1992
messages.content: I stand by this: feedback is always useful, whether it’s negative or positive. Sure, you can’t act on every single piece of feedback; partly because many people have absolutely no clue how the models actually work, thinking "copy-paste bots" constitute good work or believing "tokens" are a form of currency here. But at least it provides a direction, especially when you know the person giving the feedback actually understands what they’re doing. And the issue of bot updates over time could be solved by something like what’s shown in that screenshot; the same bot, different versions with timestamps; which would resolve the problem of having to buy it again. As a creator, you’re limited by what the platform allows you to do. That’s why; and also because there’s no real way to get feedback I usually forget about a bot the moment I upload it; I’ve done my job, and there’s nothing more I can do. But getting back to feedback: I can’t categorize everything simply as positive or negative; certainly not with a mere thumbs-up or thumbs-down. But no matter how harsh the feedback might be, I could at least work with it and keep it in mind for next time. Sure, for some narcissistic creators here, negative feedback might feel like bullying or a personal attack, but ultimately; especially for creators who take pride in their work; it would be an incredibly valuable tool.

messages.author: dragon GRaf
messages.content:
hey there i looked into it a bit more while i was working on other things:

What I found:
• Bots expose `createdAt`
• They also expose `updatedAt`, but that changes from things like message-count updates too, so it isn’t a reliable “bot edited” date
• I haven’t found a native version-history API or `publishedAt` yet (doubt i will tbh)

The good news is QoL could probably build a local version system itself.

Since QoL already has profile backups, it could hash only the creator-controlled fields like greeting, personality, scenario, tags, avatar, lorebooks, etc.

If that content hash changes, QoL could create a new version and even show what changed.

So something like:

Version 5 — Sep 18
Changed: Greeting, Tags

Version 4 — Sep 14
Changed: Personality

Then possibly compare or restore old versions too. (no promises on the restore tho)

Main limitation: it would only track versions from the point QoL starts recording them. I haven’t found a way to recover all old historical versions from SpicyChat itself yet.
